  • Chart reading

When timeframes seem to disagree

Price can be falling on the 1H chart while the rising structure holds on the 1D chart. This is not a contradiction but the same price read at two different scales. When each reading is stated with the timeframe it belongs to, both pictures can be true.

Is there really a contradiction?

Each timeframe describes a span of time of a different length. The 1H chart shows the swings of the last few days; the 1D chart shows the structure of the last few months. So "price is falling" and "the trend is up" can both be true at once: one is said on the hourly scale, the other on the daily scale.

The apparent contradiction usually appears when the timeframe drops out of the sentence. A single verdict such as "the market is falling", without saying on which scale, ignores one of the two readings.

Why both can be true

An uptrend does not move in a straight line; there are pullbacks along the way. A single pullback swing on the 1D chart can look like a small downtrend of lower highs and lows on the 1H chart.

A 1H decline does not mean the 1D structure has broken. The reference for a rising 1D structure is the last important low on the 1D chart. As long as the 1H decline stays above that low, both readings hold together. If a 1D candle closes below that low, the 1D reading can change too.

Common situations

1H falling, 1D structure intact

The 1H chart shows lower highs and lows, but price is above the last important low on the 1D chart. The 1H decline can be read as a pullback inside the 1D trend.

The 1H decline reaches the 1D low

The 1H decline reaches the zone where the last important 1D low sits. What decides it here is where the 1D candle closes relative to that zone.

1D sideways, 1H trending

Price moves back and forth in a range on the 1D chart while clear trends show on the 1H chart. These trends are often moves from one edge of the range to the other.

Stating a reading with its timeframe

  1. Put the timeframe in front of each observation. Written as separate sentences, "1H: lower highs and lows" and "1D: rising structure" no longer contradict each other.
  2. Say which timeframe a level comes from. "The last important 1D low" and "the last 1H low" are different levels and carry different weight.
  3. Write what would change the reading. For example: "If a 1D candle closes below the zone of the last important low, the 1D structure may have changed too."
  4. Avoid a single overall verdict. Instead of "the market is falling", say on which scale it is falling and what is happening on the larger scale.

What it shows, what it does not prove

What it shows

  • That different timeframes describe the same price at different scales
  • Where in the larger structure a move on a smaller timeframe sits
  • Which level could change the reading on the larger timeframe

What it does not prove

  • Which timeframe will prove right in the end
  • That the decline on the smaller timeframe will be short-lived, or that it will break the larger structure
  • That a move will certainly continue when the timeframes agree

The MarketLevelMap view

How it relates to zones

Apparent conflicts often become clearer near a higher-timeframe zone. If price falling on the 1H chart is approaching a support zone from the 1D chart, the two readings meet in one place: the 1H decline is testing that zone.

Reading the zone as a band helps here too. 1H candles entering the band do not show that the 1D structure has broken; what changes the 1D reading is a 1D close beyond the band's far edge.

An example statement

"1D: rising structure holds; the last important low sits in a support zone. 4H: the pullback continues. 1H: lower highs and lows, price approaching the 1D zone." Each sentence belongs to its own timeframe, so none contradicts another.

Often confused with

  • Pullback or reversal?A decline on a smaller timeframe can be a pullback on a larger one. For it to count as a reversal, the structure on the larger timeframe needs to change too.
  • When does a trend count as changed?A change of direction on the 1H chart does not mean the 1D trend has changed. A trend change is stated on the timeframe the trend is read on.

Key points

  • Different timeframes describe different spans of time; both can be true.
  • A decline on a smaller timeframe can be a pullback on a larger one.
  • The larger structure is judged by its own timeframe's close and its last important low or high.
  • Stating each reading with its timeframe removes the apparent contradiction.
